answer: Behavioral Lagoon Clustering detects duplicates after the fact by grouping accounts whose transaction timing, counterparties, and idle periods match a latent pattern; pairs exceeding a similarity threshold get merged. On a dune of historical activity, a sybil cluster leaves correlated traces that independent agents rarely produce. Each false identity must then sustain a distinct voyage of organic usage across weeks, costing real time and coordination overhead per account rather than a one-time fee.
